translations.text: An explanation of the birth of our Lord Christ in the flesh.
With the strength of our Lord Jesus Christ, we begin to write the volume of explanations composed by the teacher of reverence for God, Mar Thomas of Edessa, and Mar Cyrus, his fellow worker.
The first, composed by Mar Thomas.
On the birth of our Lord Christ in the flesh.
Chapter One. Addressed to the person who asked him to put it in writing.
Chapter Two. What the main topics of the explanation are.
Chapter Three. An examination of why we celebrate this feast.
Chapter Four. What good things have been given to us through our Lord Jesus Christ.
Chapter Five. Why these good things had not been revealed until now.
Chapter Six. It was necessary for there to be a mediator through whom we would receive these good things from God.
Chapter Seven. For what reasons God took nothing else at this time for his revelation, but only the ordinary human being, our Lord Christ.
Chapter Nine. Why our Lord’s humanity was taken not from the earth, but from a virgin, without intercourse with a man.
Chapter Ten. Why God arranged for our Lord’s humanity to be conceived in the season of Nisan.
Chapter Eleven. An exhortation concerning good conduct.

Chapter One. Addressed to the person who asked him to put it in writing. Your helpful advice, together with that of the distinguished brothers in our community, and your gracious command, given along with theirs,
O chosen one of God, Mar Moses the reader, gave rise to conflicting thoughts within me and occupied me with various concerns.
For you commanded me: “That explanation which you delivered after our holy master Mar Aba the Interpreter, concerning the glorious birth of our Lord and our [?], Christ—
commit it to writing as well.” I am afraid to undertake this, lest I be considered unskilled and altogether insignificant
by those who love to find fault, with or without cause. Yet I am also afraid not to carry out the command,
lest I disobey the command and scorn your advice, [?] people who say everything with the aim of reverence for the living God.
But while I was reflecting on these thoughts and others like them,
I decided that it was better for me to satisfy your wishes, leaving others to say whatever they please.
Nor would I, out of fear of envious words, which can do no harm before God, give you—who please Christ through good will and perfect conduct—
a reason to complain about me because I had not obeyed your command. Therefore, as I ask Christ for the help that comes from your acceptable prayers,
I now devote myself to fulfilling your wishes, asking this of you yourselves before anything else.
And from those who may happen to encounter these writings, I ask that you take no offense at me in any way, as though I thought myself
capable of conveying the full force of everything our teacher said on this subject, and of presenting it just as he himself expressed it,
when I undertook to speak about it or put it in writing. Rather, think this of my words, as I myself also acknowledge:
that this whole work of mine is inferior to our teacher’s, and serves only to lead someone from these words to his,
as from an image to its original, and as from a shadow to the body on which its existence depends.
And just as there is no use in lighting a little lamp where the sun’s rays are spread, so these words of mine become useless
when our teacher’s words shine with the brilliance of their meanings. For greater benefit, therefore, I distinguish the main points through which the entire discussion proceeds.
Then I begin to say what the order of each of them requires within the subject itself.
For your wisdom and understanding know that those who are about to travel a road of some miles,
which they have never known accurately before, are greatly helped by receiving signs and landmarks along the road before they proceed on their journey.
For in this way, if they pay attention, they can travel easily, without going astray, from sign to sign and from landmark to landmark, until the end of the road.
And if this is so, it is clear that it is all the more helpful for those who wish to receive a discourse of some length
to learn, before anything else, what the main points of its subject are. For if this is done, when they are required to speak,
even if they do not have the writings available for recitation, from which they could recall the whole discourse,
nevertheless, because they have already learned the number and identity of all the main points, they can speak easily, even if they leave out some of the intervening discourse.
Chapter Two: What the Main Points of the Subject Are. For although it is clear to everyone that this feast we celebrate today is the feast of Christ’s birth,
the mind does not rest content merely to learn that this feast is the feast of our Lord’s birth. Rather, it often goes on to inquire
why we celebrate it as well. And when we examine the matter and discover that it is because of the great blessings given to us through our Lord Christ,
who was born today for all creatures, so that his blessings toward us may be emphasized,
as we recall them and fulfill the will of their giver [?], we are required to say what these blessings are. And after we have recounted and explained them,
we are asked why blessings of this kind are beneficial to everyone, to the point that we even give up our lives for them.
And another question is asked: could these [?] blessings not have been brought to us from God without anything acting as an intermediary?

And when we have further shown that something was absolutely necessary through which we might be prepared to receive them, we are asked why he was not revealed through anything else, but only through a human being.
And when we have shown the many things that required the taking of a human being from among us, another question arises:
if, for these reasons, a human being was absolutely necessary, then he alone would have been sufficient for our salvation. And so we explain.
The divine plan necessarily required that God should also be in him, so that it might be known that a mere human being could not save us.

Nor could we receive from God, without some intermediary, the blessings prepared for us. But once it becomes clear that it is because of the blessings given to us through our Lord Christ that we celebrate the feast of his birth today,
the blessings are revealed for what they are, and the question of why he was not revealed before that time also finds a ready answer.
It also becomes clear that some intermediary was necessary for their revelation, and that this intermediary was none other than a human being.
Yet he was not a mere human being, but one in whom was God, who has power over everything. Concerning what he accomplished for our salvation through his divine plan, we must ask why
God did not take this human being from the earth, as he did the first Adam. Or, if it was necessary for him to be born of a woman, why was he born of a virgin without a man's seed?
After the reason for this has been explained, it remains to ask why God arranged for him to be conceived in the season of Nisan, and what we understand from his being born at this time.
Then, after these things, we will bring the whole discussion to a close, adding to it a little exhortation suitable for strengthening and correcting our listeners.
Chapter Three. An examination of why we celebrate this feast of the holy birth—that is, this feast which we celebrate today and which the holy Church observes everywhere with great joy.
It is clear that it celebrates the birth of Christ our Lord. For this is proclaimed with one accord by the mouths of all who can speak, men and women alike,

from little children to the elderly. But we must ask this: is it because of the novelty of the manner of his birth, which took place without sexual union, that we take time off today and rest for this feast,

marveling at the power that was able to form him from the Virgin Mary without a man's seed? It is certainly known that this is a great and exalted thing: that a virgin should give birth without union with a man.
But however extraordinary it is as a display of power, this alone, without the other things we are about to mention, would not have been sufficient to become the reason for this feast everywhere.
For we see other extraordinary things that happened to certain people when they came into being.
And because no other consequences followed from the manner in which they were formed, it is right that no feast is held for their birth.
Such are the cases of Adam, Eve, Isaac, and others like them. Indeed, each of these is more worthy of wonder than the next,
and magnificently proclaims divine power. Let us first consider the case of Isaac: how great a thing it is for a son to come from a woman who is both barren and old!
For either condition, on its own, would have been enough to prevent nature from bearing fruit, let alone when both were present:
old age and barrenness together. But someone may say, 'He came from seed.' And what can seed accomplish in barrenness and old age?
For it would be a great miracle if someone sowed any kind of seed on rock, or threw it into a fiery furnace, or suspended it in water
or in the air, and obtained fruit from any of these. Likewise, even if someone were to deposit seed ten thousand times amid old age and barrenness,
it would be a great miracle for a son to come from a place where even one of these conditions was present—let alone here, where both were present in Sarah.
In the case of blessed Mary, then, one thing was missing from the natural order: receiving seed.
But in Sarah's case there were both, as I said: old age and barrenness. It is more believable that the earth should sprout without being sown than that fruit should be produced by
grains of wheat that fall into a fiery furnace—even though difficult and easy things are alike to God.
For since our power is limited, we do not work equally easily with materials of clay and bronze. But for God, nothing is harder than anything else.
For his power is unlimited, and his command alone is sufficient for everything.
By comparison, that is, from our standpoint, even the case of Isaac deserves wonder, but that of Eve deserves still more. For in her case there was no belly, no womb, and no seed,
but a rib taken from the side—and this, moreover, from a male—from which a woman came into being, not over a long time through measured, gradual growth,
but she suddenly stood there, in the blink of an eye, fully grown. Yet the case of Adam is more wonderful even than this.

For she came into being as a living being from a living being, and as a being with senses from a being with senses. Adam, however, came into being alive, rational, and possessing senses from earth, which shares in none of these things.
If, then, these things too are wonders, and each one is more wonderful than the other,
[?] the Church celebrates a feast like this today in every region with joy alone.
But it is clear that we do not celebrate this feast with our attention fixed on these acts of creation. For neither did the Magi, when moved by divine grace
to come up and worship him, offer him gifts that pointed to this in any way, but gold, myrrh, and frankincense.
Frankincense indicated that this one who was born is God's temple, and that in him the Godhead would be worshiped by all rational beings, without bodily form, as in an indestructible temple.
And gold showed that henceforth all people ought to accept his counsels and commandments and obey him with all their strength.
And myrrh made known that through his death he would conquer death and gain a kingdom that cannot be shaken in any way.
It is clear, moreover, that they offered him these things because they had been instructed by a divine command. And again, when the angel appeared to the shepherds and brought them the good news,
he did not boast to them that our Lord had been born of a virgin. Rather, what did he say to them? “I bring you good news of great joy,
which will be for the whole world.” And why? He said, “Today a Savior has been born to you, who is the Lord Messiah, in the city of David.”
He mentioned the city of David to show that through this one who was born today, God's promises to the fathers were being fulfilled.
And through him all the nations would be blessed, according to the promises made to Abraham: “Through your offspring all the nations will be blessed.”
With this, in the course of his words, he also connected and joined the promise made to David: “I will seat one of the offspring of your body on your throne.”
“And his kingdom will have no end.” “The Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and his kingdom will have no end.”
He called him “Lord” because he is Lord of all created things through his union with God the Word.
For it says, “God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Messiah.” And he called him “Messiah”
because he had been set apart and chosen for this. He is the true Messiah, since all those before him were anointed with the oil prescribed by the Law,
but he was anointed with the Holy Spirit. “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.”
And he called him “Savior” because through him we were to be saved from sin, death, corruption, and slavery to Satan.
Thus it is a joy for the whole world of the nations, who are deemed worthy of belonging to God's household,
and for the people of Israel, since the promises made to their ancestors are put into effect, and all alike are delivered from all the afflictions of this world.
It is clear that the angels also share in our joy, since they too rejoice greatly at our change for the better.
But [?], the holy church commemorates John the Baptist every year for this reason: because they were ministered to through him,
and because of his perfect and exalted conduct and his death for the sake of reverence for God. As we bring to mind all these things about him,
let us take care to imitate them as far as possible, so that we may be deemed worthy to attain with him the enjoyment of heavenly blessings.
We do this when we celebrate the commemoration of all the holy fathers and of those who suffered martyrdom for Christ, each one in his proper order,
and for this very purpose that I mentioned before. So, when we celebrate this glorious and honored feast of the birth of Christ our Lord,
we do not merely look outwardly at this novel manner of his birth, which took place without sexual union. We will explain the reason for this later.
Rather, we celebrate because of these inexpressible blessings that have been given to all creation through Christ our hope,
so that, as we recall them and receive instruction about them, we may bring our conduct into harmony with the will of the one who gave them,
and may be deemed worthy to ascend to heaven and to share in those blessings reserved for those who believe rightly and conduct themselves in keeping with their faith.
Chapter Four: What the blessings are that have been given to us through our Lord Christ.
What, then, are these blessings bestowed on us through our Lord Christ, to celebrate which we gather today as we observe this feast?
It is necessary to explain. We learn about them from the holy angels, who cried out with great joy at the time of our Savior's birth, saying:
"Glory to God in the heights, and peace on earth, and good hope for humanity."
These three statements briefly make known all the blessings given to us through our Lord Christ. For the holy angels are our fellow creatures,
and when they saw that we had fallen from the health of reverence for God, had been seized by the sickness of idol worship, and had become thoroughly diseased through the service of demons,
and had rotted through the ugliness of our deeds, they were grieved and angry, and were reluctant to do even one [?] of the things necessary and useful for our preservation.
Instead, they wanted to cut us off like diseased limbs and cast us out of their fellowship, had not God, the good Lord of all,
subjected them in the hope of our correction and our return to him, as it is written: "Creation was subjected to futility,
not willingly, but because of the one who subjected it in hope." For they considered their labor on our behalf futile and unprofitable,
when we did not persevere in reverence for God, our Creator and benefactor. They endured in the hope of [?] things to come, continuing [?] in their service on our behalf,
since he had confirmed in them the hope of our change for the better through the cry of Abel's blood, the taking away of Enoch, and the ascent of Elijah,
and through the fact that God never neglected, at any time or from generation to generation, to arrange the things that would help bring about our salvation and our return to the truth.

It was therefore fitting for them, as healthy members of creation, to remain sound in their love for their Lord, zealous against those who provoke him and looking forward to the hope of better things.
The good things ordained for all creation through Christ our Lord were being revealed by God.
With great joy they cried out, saying, “Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth, and good hope for humanity!”
“Until now,” they said, “the praise that humanity owed to God had been withheld, and mute idols were being worshiped.
Satan was being served, demons were rejoicing, and evil spirits were exulting, while human beings were becoming vile and blameworthy.
They readily committed every kind of evil through their inclination toward shameful things, under the influence of the devil.
But now, through this one who has been born from David’s offspring according to the divine promises, there is being returned to God
the praise that everyone owes him. He is acknowledged as exalted and superior to everything in his being, the maker and benefactor of all.
Human beings are being gathered from the dispersion of idol worship. They are coming into harmony and turning away from the service of demons. The evil spirits are put to shame; the devil falls.
Human beings stand upright and please their maker through knowledge of the truth and virtuous conduct, and they receive correction for all their former shameful deeds.
And because of all these things, there is peace on earth. For,” they said, “human beings are turning away from worshiping the work of their own hands.
They worship God with exaltation, the maker of both us and them, conducting themselves according to his will.” They also promise tranquility, peace, and reconciliation on earth.
For the maker had been angry with his creatures, and punishment had been threatened against all humanity in proportion to their deeds.
But now, through this one who has been born, he shows reconciliation and restraint toward them.
“We angels, too, had been angry with them, like servants zealous for their master, workers subject to their benefactor.
And the more they strive to please the maker of us all, the more we increase our love for them.
In this way we also extend our diligence for their benefit, and we hold them close as healthy members.
We love them as beloved fellow servants.” Moreover, all the nations that had been divided against one another—
one worshiping the sun, another the moon, another the stars, and another something else—
while their hostility toward one another also grew frenzied in keeping with the differences among those they called gods,

all attain harmony and the love that comes from reverence for God, together with the people of Israel, from whom they had also been estranged, excluded from fellowship with God’s holy ones and all his blessings.
Like scattered limbs, they gather in love and harmony into one body devoted to the worship of God,
as all their former division is dissolved. The human being himself also attains unending peace within himself.
For since his body is mortal and his soul immortal, how opposed [?] mortal things are to immortal things!
Likewise, the activity of the body is opposed to the soul. For the soul, since it is exalted, discerning, and immortal,
And it receives knowledge of God and instruction in his commandments, and inclines toward the practice of virtue.
But the body, which is irrational, undiscerning, and mortal, clings to visible things and is held fast by love for them.
Consequently, a human being has an unceasing struggle with himself. This struggle is resolved through our Lord Christ,
when he makes the body immortal and uproots from it all its attachment to passing things.
At the same time, he decrees steadfastness for the soul, so that it may be able to do God's will without difficulty
and please him without hindrance. He promises all this abundance of peace when human beings turn toward their Maker
and praise and exalt him alone as the source of all good things, earnestly striving to please him through virtuous conduct.
Between the Creator and his creatures; and our [?], angels with human beings; and all the nations with one another and with Israel;
and that of a human being with himself. After all these things, to expect anything else, except the hope of heavenly blessings.
For there is good hope for human beings. Confidence, it says, now takes hold, and good hope abounds: hope for the uprooting of sin,
for freedom from demons and the devil, for the undoing of death, for the abolition of corruption, and for resurrection from the dead,
for the gift of immortality, for a share in incorruptibility, for the grace of adoption as children, for ascent into heaven,
and for fellowship with all God's holy ones, granted to us in those heavenly blessings that never pass away or cease.
These, then, are the blessings given to us by our Lord Christ, my honored brother,
which we celebrate together, as it were, in this feast today. They have been spoken of in the explanation of those passages from which they were drawn.
And what could have been better and more excellent for all the nations than to know God, their Creator and the source of all their blessings?
Clearly, nothing. For all the good things of this world, even if they are found where there is no fear of God, do not have the same effect.
But where there is fear of God, demonstrated in confession and deeds, even if some slight affliction should be found in one aspect of our condition,
nevertheless, all visible and comforting things come together, especially after our departure from this world.
For when someone wishes to go to the royal court, but as he begins his journey strays from the road and goes out into a desolate wilderness,
however many provisions he may be carrying, they run out and are lost, and all that remains for him is to die,
without reaching the place he had undertaken to go. So it is with someone who strays from the road—the straight road and the true fear of God:
all the provisions for his life, even if he has them, perish, and he does not reach the kingdom that comes from God, but falls into unending punishment from God.
For even if he has deeds that seem good, he is like someone who digs a well in the ground
and goes down deep, yet however far down he goes, he finds no source of water. For idols have no power to benefit those who worship them.
But look, he says, he does his good deeds in God's name, even though he admits that the one who bears that name is not God.
And what benefit comes from this? Clearly, none at all. For suppose someone takes along the payment he owes to the kingdom for some matter,
and, while going to pay it of his own free will, sees some idle men who are in the habit, in various places, of seating one of their number in royal attire and speaking before him.
If he is deceived by them and goes and lays before them the money he owes to the kingdom, will he not, after a time, by order of the true king,
be arrested and imprisoned, without having deducted from his debt what he gave to the man who is merely called a king, although he is not a king?
In the same way, someone who takes all his acts of worship and almsgiving owed to the true God
and lays them before those who are not gods, but through the activity of demons are called by a name that is not theirs,
will not have a single one of these credited to him when he comes before the judgment of God, the maker of all, who alone is God.
To him alone worship is owed by all created beings. Therefore, everyone who has not acquired knowledge of God
loses everything that gives him joy, even if these things are available to him for a time. In this way all his labor becomes fruitless.
And his deeds that seem good turn out to be of no benefit to him. And his deeds that seem good
turn out to bring him no reward, and he falls into eternal punishment. This is what all the nations were awaiting before the coming of Christ.
It is clear, however, that even for the people of Israel, although they had a close relationship with God,
the coming of Christ our Lord brought them too a great benefit: they were raised above a child's way of life,
and they too were deemed worthy of complete knowledge of the Holy Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who are known in unity.

For they were no different from someone who calls the soul and the sun each 'one,' without acknowledging that the latter has such things as heat and radiance, while the former possesses mind and reason.
And if we feel great joy when we wean an infant from milk and introduce him to solid food,
how much more worthy of rejoicing is this: that the Israelites, together with all the nations, have attained complete knowledge of the Holy Trinity!
But in shameful conduct too, in attachment—in attachment to earthly things [?]—they were all equally held fast in this way.
As [?], they knew God and did not hope for good things from him. Like an infant who clings to the breast at the time of his weaning,
so they clung to earthly things. But our Lord God established in his gospel the expectation of things to come,
and they despised and scorned everything belonging to this world. This too is a chief good when it is accompanied by the fear of God.
For a rational person held captive by love of these passing possessions is like a tongue or an eye on which someone has hung some sacred object as an ornament. Not only is this no ornament for them,
but it also [?] each one of them from the beneficial activity it possesses for itself and for the whole body.
And he is like a child to whom a fig that gives him a little pleasure is more welcome than precious stones, whose great value he does not understand.
There is therefore nothing so good and beneficial for human beings as knowing God with complete knowledge and devoting themselves solely to his commandments.
And they rise above attachment to visible things, for in this way God also comes to be pleased with them.
And angels will care for them, and they will acquire love for one another and be found worthy of the unfading blessings in the new and indestructible world.
If, however, there are some who even now have not believed in Christ, just as there are those who have believed but do not fulfill his commandments, this is not his doing.

For his part, look: the light of the knowledge of him shines upon everyone, and the banquet of his blessings is prepared for everyone. But it stands as an accusation against those who have not believed, or who have believed but have not acted.
They are like someone who stands beneath the sun and closes his eyes so as not to see, and like someone who is invited to a banquet but keeps his feet from going.
Chapter Five: Why these blessings were not revealed until now.
Let us now move on to discuss the question before us: why the coming of Christ did not take place until this time,
since it has been shown to be so beneficial to all rational beings. Was it perhaps because God did not know of it until now?
Or, though he possessed knowledge of it, did he lack the power to accomplish it? Or, though he possessed both—I mean knowledge and power—
did he begrudge us our blessings, as an evil being would, and therefore delay it until now?
For a person is prevented from doing good either by ignorance, by weakness, or by wickedness,
when he himself is the cause of its delay. But that God knew from the beginning that he would raise up our Lord Christ
is clear from his advance announcements about his coming and about the blessings given to us through him, made long ago to the fathers in his promises
and through the prophets among the people of Israel. And just as we cannot maintain that he does not now know that he will raise us from the dead
because he has not raised us already, so neither can we suppose that he did not know that he would reveal our Lord Christ because he had not put this into effect from the beginning.
For although he had not accomplished it in deed, he certainly announced it concerning him.
And his foreshadowings were depicted among the people of old. But let us go back and examine whether this can also be seen at the beginning of creation.
For unless he had brought creation into existence with a view to things to come, he would not even have created two heavens,
suited to the way of life of both worlds. And how can one suppose, moreover, that he lacks the power?
For renewing us after we have come into being is not as difficult as bringing us into being when we did not exist at all,
when there was nothing from which to fashion us and give us existence. And it is known that he is good. For if he had been evil from the beginning,
he would never have changed to goodness, since God possesses all his attributes without change.
Or is this not an indescribable blessing: that when we could not come into being by our own will,
he not only granted us existence, as he did to stones and pieces of wood, but also raised us above the animals that cannot speak?
And he made us discerning and rational, and generously gave us authority over all these visible things.
If, then, he was good, knowledgeable, and powerful from the beginning, there was nothing else preventing him from bringing about everything good for us,
except our own weakness, which could not receive all these things together without training.
With divine wisdom taking this into account, his inexpressible grace guided us in whatever way was beneficial to us.
For if one of us has a son or a pupil whom he wishes to teach a craft that he himself knows,
does he not lead him from little things to great ones? And if, for example, he wishes to teach him the religious life,
he first teaches him the alphabet, and then letter combinations and words, so that he may learn and spell them out. After these come the Psalms, through which he also learns to read.
And he assigns him a text to copy until he learns the forms of the letters. Then, after all these things, he also gives him books of interpretation to read,
so that he may grasp the meaning of the divine Scriptures. But if, before the pupil learns to read, someone forces him to explain passages, it is clear that, while the pupil gains no benefit,
the teacher too appears to be mad: without laying a foundation, he strives to put up a roof.
If, then, we who are mortal and limited know how to manage our affairs in an orderly way, dealing with our children and pupils according to our knowledge and ability,
but measuring out our teaching to them according to their capacity to receive it,

how much more fitting was it for the Lord, who is wiser and better than all, to measure out everything in his providence for our benefit and according to our strength, rather than according to his own foreknowledge and power
in his dealings with us, but according to our own weakness. And let us consider that inexpressible wisdom:
how, from the beginning, it led our nature step by step toward complete knowledge, like a compassionate father and a teacher who comes down to his pupils’ level.
Grace guided those first generations, from Adam to Noah, according to one order,
as at the first stage of children’s learning, when the alphabet is written out for them, arranging everything needed both to deter them and to encourage them to keep away from evil
and turn to doing good. In the same way, we too sometimes frighten them,
so that by every means we may lead them toward what is right, taking our cue from them
as to whether we should deal with them in this way or that. So too God our maker, who has always shown fatherly compassion toward our race in his immeasurable grace,
sometimes brought punishment upon wrongdoers, as upon Adam and Eve at the very beginning, and upon Cain, who killed his brother,
so that, as this report was passed on to those who came after them, they might be deterred from turning to shameful deeds. We learn this also from Lamech,
who, when he had killed a man unintentionally, was seized with great fear, lamenting his own plight and mourning in the presence of his wives,
as someone who was about to receive punishment from God many times greater than Cain’s, because he had killed even after learning what terrible sentence the murderer had been handed over to.
And at another time he made the blood of righteous Abel cry out from the ground after he had died.
To show how much care God has for those who fear him: even after their death, he listens to their voice and exacts vengeance for them from their oppressors.
Through this, to encourage everyone to strive to love him and take care to keep his commandments, just as we see that Enoch did, who was thus accounted righteous.
So that we too may be worthy of being taken away from among human beings, and of the dwelling toward which nature had advanced a little before him.
He brought the waters of the flood upon those earlier people because of their filthiness, their wickedness, and their evil deeds.
He rescued Noah and those with him, giving them laws in which their predecessors had not been instructed.
They were to eat everything, like green plants, after pouring out its blood, which serves as the soul in irrational animals. Similarly, after a child has learned the alphabet,
we write out the letters and names for him so that he may learn to spell. Then again, after no short time, he chose Abraham, the chief of the patriarchs,
and gave him the law of circumcision and explicit promises concerning his descendants—something higher than what had been given to Noah and his household.
When his descendants had been tried by many hardships in the land of Egypt, he brought them out of there through various mighty deeds.
He gave them various laws in writing. Similarly, after our children and pupils have learned to spell,
we write out psalms for them so that through these they may also learn to read; then we also give them a text to copy.
After our nature had thus reached full stature, so to speak, and had passed through and been trained in those earlier teachings,
he then brought about the coming of Christ, which teaches perfect knowledge and gives hope and the promise of the good things to come.
This is like someone who, after the lessons we have listed, gives his son books of interpretation to read, so that he may [?] the meaning and sense of what he learned before.
Nor did he neglect to do the same things in every generation as he had done for those earlier people,
bringing punishment upon the wicked and sinners, making those of his household glorious and renowned, and ordering things well for the purpose we mentioned earlier.
It is as when someone has ten pupils, for example, who are all at the same stage of learning the alphabet.
One of them neglects his lesson and goes out to play with [?]; another begins eating and drinking without attending to his reading; another dozes off and sleeps.
Still others occupy themselves together in idle talk and empty stories, paying no attention to the instructions given for their learning,
while the rest learn as they should and value practice in their lessons above everything else, according to their teacher’s wishes.
When they are called upon to recite, they receive punishment—not because they have failed to learn to read and understand the meaning of books,
but because they have not recited the alphabet, so to speak, on a level with their companions. So too God, the Lord of all,
when he enters into judgment and calls human beings to account for their deeds, does not demand of Adam and his household why they were not circumcised,
nor of Noah and his household why they did not keep the Sabbath. Rather, to put it briefly, he calls each generation to account in comparison with its contemporaries,
repaying everyone according to their deeds, in keeping with the time in which they lived and the laws that God had given in their days.
And just as God did not demand from earlier generations what belonged to later generations, because they did not yet exist,
so likewise it was not fitting for human nature to remain at one stage without advancing, just as it does not benefit a child to study nothing but the alphabet until old age.
Therefore, Christ’s coming did not harm those earlier generations by not taking place sooner, since the conduct taught by Christ was not required of them. But it has benefited us beyond measure,
because it turned us from error toward God, perfected us through complete knowledge, and promised us the good things to come, as I said above.
And it is clear that it took place at this time with great wisdom. For if it had been revealed earlier, the earlier generations would not have been capable of receiving it,
just as someone who has only now begun learning to spell does not have enough knowledge to grasp the meaning of books of interpretation.
But if someone says that God could have implanted all knowledge in us without gradual training,
from the very beginning, that person is mistaken. In trying to spare himself effort, he places himself among irrational animals,
which possess naturally, without training, everything they have. So too eunuchs possess chastity.
For this reason we do not say that any one of these kinds deserves praise or blame, a good reward or punishment.
The same would also have happened to us if, without training, we had received from our very formation that life free from need and change. For this reason it was necessary for us to exist first.
It was necessary for someone undergoing training and learning to be led from small things to great ones. But someone says, “Look, he created us changeable!”
“And for this reason we sin. Why, then, does he judge us when we sin?” But who is judged for being changeable? Certainly no one!
For changeability and sin are not the same thing. We call it changeability
when someone, wishing to act, is equally capable of turning in either direction. But we consider it sin
when someone judges with discernment and learns from God’s commandments—or is at least capable of judging and knowing—that he ought not to do a certain thing,
yet neglects and condemns his own discernment, despises the divine commandments, and does it for his temporary pleasure or out of resentment toward his fellow,
or for any other reason, doing something else that he himself understood, or could have understood, ought not to be done,
and which the divine commandment also forbade him to do. Therefore, God does not judge a person for being capable of turning toward what is wrong,
but for doing it when he could have restrained himself from doing it, and for failing, for whatever reason, to do what was right.
“But,” someone says, “if he had not created us changeable, we would not have sinned at all.” But neither would we have become righteous at all.
For just as, if he had created you so that you could not offend God, you would have had no sin, so likewise, if he had formed you so that you could not sin,
you would not have had any righteousness either. But now, since you are equally capable of turning toward either one whenever you wish,
you can have both sin and righteousness: sin, because although you could have pleased God, like the other people who have pleased him throughout the generations and fulfilled his will,
you instead went after your own desires, without caring about what was right.
And righteousness too, because, when you were able to do good deeds, you valued duty and the fear of God above everything.
Thus, because of the former you were blamed and receive punishment, but because of the latter you are praised and judged worthy to enjoy good things.
But if we describe dumb animals or sentient natures as liable to change, we describe them this way figuratively,
instead of saying that they are changeable by nature. But in the case of rational beings, liability to change is spoken of in the sense I explained above.
But if you say that God could have done both things for us—made us incapable of change from the very beginning,
and also implanted in us discerning knowledge of all our duties without experience of other things—it is clear that such a person does not understand what he is saying,
and does not even know what he is asking. For everything that enters our thoughts as existing, however it exists, we find to exist in one of these ways.
Outside these, nothing exists in any other way. Outside these, nothing exists in any other way, nor can it exist.
There is God, the maker of us all. And there are all rational beings, divided into two orders: visible and invisible.
And there are all the dumb animals. And there are natures that are neither living nor sentient. But God has no equal, nor has he ever had one.
For how can something made be like its maker, when it could not even bring itself from nonexistence into existence?
How can something made be without a beginning? For it came into being at a particular point, and before it came into being it did not exist.
Or how can something whose coming into being has a definite time have an unlimited nature?
For someone whose nature nothing contains, neither time nor duration of any kind can rightly be conceived as preceding his existence.
For all these things belong to God alone: to bring all natures into existence when they do not exist,
while he exists truly and eternally, before all the ages and mountains that can enter our thoughts;
and for his nature also to be unlimited and boundless, indeed incomprehensible. All these things also entail his knowing things
without receiving knowledge from anyone else or gaining experience of anything; and his being as he is at all times, at whatever time anyone might conceive,
without undergoing any change of any kind. These, then, are God's unique attributes, and for any created being to attain them
is impossible. For wherever one of these is found, their necessary connection requires that all of them be found.
It is therefore great presumption, and Satan's own arrogance, for someone to say that it would have been better if we had been incapable of change or alteration,
and had possessed discerning knowledge of everything from the very beginning. For such a person knows the rank in which he is seeking to stand.
How much punishment this deserves, if anyone can say! Certainly, whoever says it deserves even to be reduced to nothing.
If, then, it was impossible for us to exist in such a rank, perhaps it was as stones, wood, and the four elements,
and things like these, which do not incline toward sin, that we wished to exist? But if you ask any rational being this,
You find them all equally rejecting it, since one does not even wish to be like the sun, which does not recognize its own house, however brightly it shines.
For it is clear that the sun possesses this fiery nature, since we can kindle fire from it in many ways if we wish.
And it is clear that fire also comes out of stone. For something hidden inside stones is plainly not alive
or capable of sensation, and no rational being desires this. And if not this, do we perhaps wish to be like irrational animals,
for which neither sin nor righteousness is determined, whatever their behavior may be?
For we do not blame the rooster, however much it mates, nor do we praise the turtledove, however faithfully it mates with only one partner.
Nor do we say that a female donkey deserves punishment, however often she conceives. Nor do we call a female mule blessed because she does not mate or conceive at all.
Likewise, we do not say that the other kinds of animals possess either sin or righteousness in their actions.
But we find that all rational beings reject this condition itself as well, just as they reject the former one.
For all these things were created for this purpose: besides providing us with knowledge and
many useful things, they also enable us to learn through them what blessedness the Creator of all has deemed us worthy of, in not creating us like one of them,
and to be grateful for his love toward our race. What, then? If it is impossible for us to be like God,
and if we do not choose to be like one of the kinds of irrational animals, or like one of the natures incapable of sensation,
what else can we say, except that we should give thanks to God in word and deed, as far as we are able,
because he has so honored us and raised us above all visible things, and has also brought us near and given us a share in what belongs to him, as was fitting?
But if someone says, “Why did he not create us in the likeness of angels?”—they too are liable to go astray, just like us.
For all the demons and the Devil belong to those ranks. Nevertheless, this was helpful for our instruction:
that we human beings should be composed of the whole creation, visible and invisible, so that we might learn through our own being, and the angels likewise through us,
that there is one God, the maker of all creatures, visible and invisible. For if this had not been so, it might have seemed
that there were as many makers as there were different natures. But now that all the varieties of creation
have been gathered by the wise Maker into one living creature, the rational human being, it is plainly known that, although the natures differ and the creatures are diverse, their Maker is one:
he who gathered and bound them all together in one human being composed of all these things. “But look,” someone says, “because we are liable to go astray, many people sin,
and for this reason they are handed over to unending punishment in Gehenna. What benefit was it for them to be rational and intelligent, if they are not deemed worthy of the good things of heaven?”
The person who says this ought to consider that those who sinned had the power not to sin, just like the others who pleased God,
since they share the same nature. But because they willingly despised and made light of the divine commandments, they are justly deprived of the blessings of heaven.
But it is far higher and nobler for someone to be in hell than to lack reason and understanding.
And if my statement is not accepted, let us consider someone who does not enjoy the delightful light of this visible sun.
Let us see which he chooses for himself: to remain as he is, or to become a donkey with large eyes and keen sight.
But someone may say that the blind man's disability is not very severe. Yet who is more wretched in this world than a leper?
Even if you ask him, you will find that he wishes to remain with the afflictions he has, rather than be transformed into a camel, for example,
or something else of that sort. In the same way, those who go to hell and fall into various punishments because of their hateful deeds
continually receive the kindness of their Maker, because he did not reduce them to nothing, as they deserved,
and did not make them like dumb animals or insensible beings. As for their being deprived of ascent to heaven and fellowship with the righteous,
they attribute this to their own actions. They have no excuse, and even in this they praise divine justice without end.
But remember also what I said above: there is knowledge of everything without experience of anything, and continuance in exactly the same state,
without any change whatever in any of our conditions. All these things must belong to God. Perhaps someone thinks this is false,
on the grounds that we believe that after the resurrection from the dead all rational beings receive perfect knowledge
and remain unchanged forever. But how far this differs from that is clear to those who know how to listen.
For I spoke of knowledge of everything without experience of anything, and of remaining in exactly the same state at all times. If anyone considers it, these things are never found in us.
For already in this world we have experienced many things and have undergone no small changes.
Therefore, even in this respect we are not divine. But this subject, my dear brother, cannot be exhausted, however much anyone says.
For if anyone examines it carefully, he can recognize how briefly I have stated everything in this chapter.
Chapter Six. On the necessity of taking an intermediary through whom we might receive those great blessings from God.
Let us now show that it was not possible to receive these blessings and benefit from them without an intermediary.

For just as, if something had been revealed from the beginning, we would not have benefited from these blessings, because we could not have understood them on account of our immaturity and the reasons we have mentioned,
so too, if at this time God, the Lord of all, had not employed an intermediary in accordance with his wisdom, their benefit would not have reached us.
For if God were visible, seeing him would itself have been sufficient for our instruction. But as he is invisible,
it is impossible to learn about him without an intermediary. For although the prophets are said to have seen the Lord, it is clear that they were not seeing his nature.
For John says, “The truth of grace came through Jesus Christ.” Explaining what he means by truth and grace, he says, “No one has ever seen God.”
And it is clear that no human being has seen, or can see, the one who dwells in light, as blessed Paul teaches with these words.
That those of former times never saw God, nor do those of later times ever see him—not human beings, you may say, but not even the invisible powers.
Everything that is [?] is seen either in part or in its entirety. For we see the earth in part, and likewise the sky and the sea.
And although we see only a part of each one of them, because our sight cannot encompass their four directions,
we say that we see the sky, the earth, and the sea. As for small things—stones, wood, and things like these, for example—because of their smallness,
we see them entirely, within their limits. It is therefore not possible to see God in part, as we see the earth and the sky,
because he is not composite and is not made up of parts. Nor, again, does he come within our sight in the manner of small things,
because he is both infinite and unbounded. And if we wished to see him as he is, we would only be longing for our own destruction.
For who could throw a little wax into a fiery furnace and find it again? Or who could throw a handful of dust into the great sea
and be able to discover [?] what became of it? And if among the things that have been made, all of which are created, there are things that dissolve and destroy one another
when they are brought near and fall into them, how much more with God, the maker of everything, who is infinite in his divinity
and indescribable in his glory! If our sight were to penetrate him completely, would we not vanish more completely than wax melts in fire,
and more completely than a handful of dust disappears in abundant water? And just as the great sea, because of its breadth and its unfathomable depth,

cannot be crossed by anyone on their own without something acting as an intermediary, such as a boat or a ship, [?] without something acting as an intermediary, through which one might be led to knowledge of the invisible one.
For if the soul, which is created and finite, cannot, because we do not see it, be known to us in its will or even in its existence without its activity in one of the body's members,
how much less could we receive teaching about the one who is the maker of everything and is incomprehensible, and learn his wishes,
without his revealing himself through one of his creatures! Rightly, therefore, did God, who desires good things,
in accordance with the overflowing riches of his grace, not make his revelation to us without something acting as an intermediary.

Instead, he took for himself a complete human being from among us for his revelation to us. Through him he taught us complete knowledge of himself and of his wishes, and promised us heavenly good things that do not pass away.
Chapter Seven: For what reasons our Lord God took nothing else at this time for his revelation,
except a human being from among us. But let us now state the reasons why a human being from among us was necessary for the divine revelation at this time.
For the question is asked: Why did God not make his revelation to us through fire, or a cloud, or one of the parts of creation,
as he did to the ancient fathers, but only through a complete human being taken from our race? We therefore say
that it was for this very reason that God did not now make his revelation to us through one of these parts:
because he had revealed himself through them to our fathers. For just as in the beginning God fashioned the whole creation part by part,
and then, when it lacked nothing, at the very end gathered it together in one human being, after whom he created nothing new.

In the same way, now too, after making himself known to our fathers in earlier generations part by part, he gathered together all the parts of all his revelations in these last times in this human being whom he took from among us.
After him he is no longer revealed through anything else, since in him all the earlier revelations were brought to completion. And he remains forever, without dissolution.
For when he wished to bring about a partial salvation and wanted to teach instruction suited to little children,
and wished to meet the need in the fullness of time, he fittingly accomplished his revelation to the learners through a part of creation.
But now that he wished to make complete salvation dawn upon all creation, and saw fit to deliver instruction complete in every respect,
he fittingly took the human being, complete in body and soul, as the bond of all creation. In him all created things, visible and invisible, are bound together.
Furthermore, because Adam, the first human being, the father of all humanity, obeyed the devil from the very beginning of his formation and transgressed the divine command,
and received from God the sentence of death, which was spread and passed on like a debt to all his offspring,
who further strengthened the sentence of death against themselves through various inventions of idol worship and assorted sins,
by trampling on love for their neighbors, scorning the honor due to parents, and also turning a blind eye to the observances of the law of Moses,
it was necessary for a human being sharing their nature, their brother from the line of Adam, the first human being, to arise,
so that, being righteous in everything and blameless in all his conduct, he might remove the sentence of death from us,
undo and abolish sin, release us from subjection to Satan and the demons, and free us from the curse of the law of Moses,
and promise us immortal life through the resurrection from the dead. For just as death came through a human being,
so too the resurrection of the dead comes through a human being. And just as all human beings die in Adam, so too all live in Christ.
And just as through the disobedience of one human being many became sinners, so too through the obedience of one human being many become righteous.
For when someone incurs a debt and has nothing with which to repay it, his property is taken from him, and even his descendants are reduced to slavery.
But if someone arises from his line who can, through his diligence, repay his father's debts, he recovers his property and frees all his brothers from subjection to sin and slavery.
So too, after Adam incurred a debt through his obedience to the devil, and he and all his descendants after him became subject to death,
God took the human being Jesus, the second Adam, from our own race, and by his grace made him blameless,
so that he might die without being guilty, since he had not sinned, and through his own freedom from guilt our debt might be canceled.
And because he died without being subject to sin, we might live—we who received the sentence of death because of sin.
For if God was crucified and died, as the heretics say, there would have been no benefit to us.
Instead, he would have saved his fellow gods. For if God is mortal, it is clear that there are also many gods like him.
But the true God shares in none of the sufferings of created beings. Yet if someone says that it is a greater act of mercy for him to die and for us to be saved,
Just as, if someone incurs a debt, another may pay on behalf of those who have been reduced to slavery and set them free, so our Lord's humanity has indeed done this.
For when he alone had proved righteous and was without blemish, he promised immortal life to all human beings, who share his nature.
It would have been easy for God, if he had considered it beneficial, to bring us all to immortal life by his command alone, even without taking a human being from among us.
But he did not do this [?] of our Lord. For when he alone had proved righteous and was without blemish, he promised immortal life to all human beings, who share his nature.
It would have been easy for God, if he had considered it beneficial, to bring us all to immortal life by his command alone, even without taking a human being from among us.

But he did not do this, so that he would not be thought to love hateful things, having saved us while we were still in our sins, without the mediation of someone from among us who had proved righteous.
Instead, by taking someone from among us and then freeing us from death and sin, he has now shown his justice and deterred us from doing hateful and evil things.
For he handed over to death the one who was not guilty, and then saved us, since a single person was sufficient for him in place of our whole race.
He revealed his indescribable mercy: although we were all obliged to be without blemish
and only then inherit immortal life [?], he promised us this because of just one who had proved righteous, so that we would not grow faint and abandon hope of changing for the better.
These reasons, however, are inferred from the ways God carries out his plan. For it is clear that this was what God saw fit to do from the very beginning:

first to make our nature subject to suffering and death, and then, at the end, after the exercise and training of our rational faculties in this world, to give us a share in immortal and unchanging life.
But so that he might bring us benefit from everything that belongs to us, he presented death, which had been placed in Adam's nature from his very formation, as having come upon us through sin,
so that we would all fear and shrink from acting against God's commandments, if disobedience does such harm
that it even dissolves the human constitution and separates a person's soul from the body.
But that immortal life, which he had determined before the foundations of the world to grant us at the proper time [?], he revealed through the man Jesus Christ.
As Paul the apostle said, there is one mediator between God and human beings, so that he might stir us all together
and urge us to love, and teach us that righteousness possesses such power that, when it is found in just one person, it gives life to countless multitudes.
This, then, was the divine will before all ages. But the way he carried out his plan benefited us in many ways, as I have said.
When someone looks into this and grasps the meaning of the Scriptures, he rightly states the reasons we have just recounted.
But there was a more compelling reason than all these for the taking on of our Lord's humanity.
For at this time, when our nature had reached full stature, so to speak, as I have said, it was necessary for it to receive complete teaching about God,
who is known in three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, equal in nature, without beginning and without end.
This could not have been revealed to rational beings through any part of creation. This is clear from the fact that, as long as revelation through such things was being given to them
by God, those people of former times did not have this knowledge, so as to learn about that glorious divine nature which is known in three persons.
And he is exalted above all composition and every restriction and boundary belonging to any place.
But some of them thought that his dwelling was in paradise, while others maintained that his dwelling was confined to heaven alone.
Others thought that the activity of his providence was restricted to Jerusalem, while they did not acknowledge the distinction of persons in the Godhead.
But now we have learned through a human being from among us that God is spirit and that he is everywhere. For wherever anyone may think of him, he is equally present everywhere.
And wherever he is present by nature, he is equally able to act. That is, the whole world is sustained in him and exists in him like a grain of sand in the hand of one of us.
And to a degree beyond expression; and that this ineffable Being exists in three persons.
For from his being called Christ, we learned about the Father who anointed him and the Holy Spirit who filled him in place of oil.
“Jesus of Nazareth,” it says, “whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power.” And again, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me.”
“For this reason he anointed me,” our Lord himself said about himself. And again, from his being named Son, we understand the eternal Son who is with his Father.
Just as, through this bread that is called the body of Christ, we are raised toward that body which is in heaven.
But any one of these parts of creation through which he revealed himself to people of old—such as fire, cloud, and the stones and timbers of the temple,
and the ark and the gold plate—could not be given the name of Son. But that our Lord’s humanity should be called the Son of God did not seem something new,
because many others had also been called this, as in, “I have begotten and brought up children,” and, “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.’”
And when they approached him and saw his deeds, which surpassed his nature, and heard the words he spoke,
“I and my Father are one,” and, “Whoever has seen me has also seen the Father,” they recognized that the eternal Son from the Father was hidden in him, performing these things through him,
and that words such as these were fitting for him. For just as, if you wave your hand, nod your head, or wink your eyes,
the soul, hidden in the body and invisible, communicates some small thing—whether someone should go, come, stand, or sit,
or something of that sort—but makes known and brings to light all its wishes and the knowledge contained in its thoughts through the tongue alone, in the same way,
when the invisible God revealed himself to people of old through one of these parts of creation, he taught them partial knowledge, according to the need that their immaturity required.
But now that he has assumed a complete human being from among us, through him he has taught us all his wishes and made himself fully known to us, as far as was possible,
like the soul, which reveals all its knowledge through the tongue and brings it out into [?]. Therefore, for this reason too, it was necessary for him to assume a human being from among us.
And again, because resurrection from the dead was being promised, and a promise of ascent into heaven was being made,

we would not have believed that either of these would be fulfilled in us unless we had seen someone from among us, sharing our nature and like us, who died, rose, and himself ascended first into heaven.
But when these things were first accomplished in someone like us, we believed that it would not be difficult for them to happen to us also, since we share the very same nature
as the one who has already received them in reality; but [?] the ascent of the righteous into heaven.
[?] that through him God was to judge all humanity, as the apostle says: “When God judges people’s secrets according to my gospel, through Jesus Christ.”
For the righteous are more deeply aware of the enjoyment of good things, and the wicked of the punishment they receive,

when they receive repayment for all their deeds from someone visible like themselves. Another point, again, concerns what follows the resurrection from the dead and the ascent of the righteous to heaven.
They will not build buildings of hewn stone, timber, cedar, and precious stones in which to worship God, as they do in this world.
Instead, he himself takes the place of a temple for them, and in him they worship the Holy Trinity without end, showing their love for God
by offering him, in him as in a temple endowed with reason, the worship they owe him, together with praise and thanksgiving.
In him they find comfort and rest. Their minds, which long to see God, rest as in a harbor when they see him as that One.
They ascend from him to the invisible One, as from an image to its [?]. For he, it says, is “the image of the invisible God.”
For if, when someone dear to us is far away, we gaze at his image and are moved with longing, how much more are the righteous comforted and glad,
and the flame of love in their minds, eagerly longing to see God their Creator and the source of all their good things, finds satisfaction
in this image endowed with reason, clothed in divine glory, exalted above them all and ruling over all created things.
For in him they see, as it were, the One who is invisible to them. In him they perceive the One who is hidden in his being, and receive assurance concerning him.
All these reasons required the honored assumption of a human being from among us, O our brother.
The sum and fulfillment of all the preceding things is the salvation of all creatures, visible and invisible;
the removal of all the afflictions that, through Adam, the first human being, were seen to rule over our nature;
the condemnation of Satan [?] receives what his deeds deserve; and that in him the righteous should show their love for God,
and in him receive assurance concerning the invisibility of their Maker and Benefactor.
Chapter Eight: That Our Lord Christ Is Not a Mere Human Being. But let us now resolve the doubt of many:
those who, when they hear us describe the distinctive properties of our Lord’s humanity and the reasons for which it was assumed,
lash out at us, saying, “Then he is a mere human being, and according to your account he alone was sufficient to save.”
They say this out of their own injustice and lack of understanding. For if they examined carefully what has been said, they would understand what we said:
that in him God the Word is revealed, together with his Father and the Holy Spirit, and in him, as in a temple endowed with reason, he is worshiped without end.
Again, in him, as in an image, he is seen by all his righteous ones. These things do not allow our Lord’s human being to be regarded as ordinary.
These statements alone are enough to show his greatness and his distinction from all created things.
Nevertheless, let us also state other reasons that show that God was in that human being who was assumed from among us.
We said above that it was necessary for him to be fully righteous and blameless in everything—in thoughts, words, and deeds.
[?] And he extended help to him in keeping with the excellence of his will.
“He was justified in the Spirit,” it says. And because he was fulfilling the law of Moses, it was necessary for its course to cease, since it had now been fulfilled.
For this reason too, it was necessary for God to be in him, because abolishing the law belonged to him alone, since he himself had given it in the beginning.
And again, after the law had ceased its course and the way of life of the new covenant was beginning,
it was necessary for those who became members of God's household through faith in him to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit for adoption as children.
For this reason too, we say that God dwelt in him, since he alone is able to give the grace of the Spirit.
Moreover, our Lord's humanity could not have risen from the dead and ascended into heaven if God had not been in him.
For he alone can grant release from death. Nor could we ourselves have received new life at the end, or the righteous have been raised to the highest heavens,
if he had been an ordinary human being. For all these reasons, then, it was necessary for God also to be in that man who was taken from the offspring of the house of David.
Just as, for those earlier reasons we mentioned, it was not permissible without [?].
Chapter Nine: Why our Lord's humanity was not taken from the earth, but from a virgin without union with a man.
But now that it has been shown that we are gathered today because of the good things given to us through our Lord Jesus Christ, and it has also become clear what those good things are,
and it has been revealed that even their not being revealed earlier was arranged with great wisdom for our benefit,
and it has also been shown that an intermediary was necessary through whom these good things would reach us—an intermediary who was none other than a human being, yet not an ordinary human being,
but one in whom God, the Lord of all and almighty, was also present—let us now explain why God did not take our Lord's humanity from the earth, as he did the first Adam,
and why he was born of a woman without union with a man. Once we have explained this,
we will turn to why God arranged for his conception to take place in the season of Nisan, and what we understand from his being born at this time.
Adding a little exhortation to this, we will bring the whole subject to a close, as I said at the beginning.
From the very beginning of our formation, we provoked anger, transgressed the divine commandments, and trampled on the judgment of our own reason,
because of our hostile inclination toward our fellow human beings. In short, throughout all our generations we have thus shown ourselves opposed to God in our words and deeds,
so that even if we had been returned to nothing, we would have deserved it [?], apart from a few who, generation after generation, were found among us like pearls in the sand.
If God had taken our Lord's humanity from the earth, as he did the first Adam, we would all then have been overcome by despair.
We would have thought that God had rejected our race because of our sins, and that we no longer had any hope of anything better.
Therefore God, whose mercy and fatherly goodness toward our race have been immeasurable from the beginning, saw fit to take him not from the earth but from our own nature.
So that we may learn that the life free from death, change, and decay that our Lord received at his resurrection from the dead is passed on to our entire race, and that we all share in it together.
For he shares our nature and is not foreign to us. For just as, because we share the nature of the first Adam, all the afflictions that he first received were passed on and spread to all of us,
so, because our Lord also shares our nature, he became the inaugurator of the good things that await us, just as Adam also was
of the afflictions here, we believe and have hope that we will all share with our Lord Christ in life free from death and change,
just as we also shared with the first Adam in the things of this world, which are full of every affliction. For it says, “Just as through Adam we all die, so through Christ we all live.”
[?] like the first Adam, or from another source, from wherever anyone might say. For it is clear that, although he was formed and born without intercourse
from Mary the virgin, nevertheless he shares the entire nature of men and women, and has a share in them all. For blessed Mary also, like all women,
came from a man and a woman. And if the woman who bore him was constituted from both groups, men and women,
he too must necessarily have a share in them all, since he was born from her who was constituted from both.
That is why the Scriptures call him the son of David and Abraham, since blessed Mary, from whom he was born, descended from their offspring.
Therefore the good things that are in him are also passed on to all human beings, to men and women alike,
because he is united with them all in nature, as I have said. As for his being formed by the Holy Spirit without intercourse with a man,

this was so that it might be known that he is the inaugurator of the new order and of the world to come, like Adam, who was formed from the earth without intercourse and became the head and father of this world.
For the one who was to become the head and inaugurator of mortal life was fittingly created from lifeless earth.
But this one, who became the inaugurator and revealer of this world [?] immortal life, was taken from living earth, Mary the virgin, without intercourse with a man.
For the newness [?] of his formation, which took place without seed, was enough to proclaim that he was the inaugurator of a new order,

the one bestowed by the resurrection of the dead, which takes place through the power of the Spirit, who also did not lack the power to form him from a virgin without intercourse, beyond the order of nature.
Chapter Ten: Why God arranged for him to be conceived in the first season.
God arranged for him to be conceived in the season of Nisan because it was also at this very season that God had made the whole creation.
For the sameness of the season taught that he himself is the very one who created in the beginning, and that he is the one who now renews creation through this one who was conceived.
Then he was born at this time according to the order of nature established by God from the very beginning. For, on the basis of the correspondence and similarity of the events themselves, we say

that, just as at this season the day—the period of light—has shortened and decreased to nine hours, and from this point onward the day, the dominion of light, begins to take back from the night its realm of darkness,
and again, no fruits of crops or trees are found among us today, for the seed is beginning to sprout, and all the trees are shedding even their leaves,
in the same way both things were seen among all human beings [?] of the coming of our Lord Christ. For the light of the knowledge of the truth had disappeared from our souls,
and the darkness of the error of idol worship had taken hold of our thoughts.
While we were deprived and stripped of all the fruits of righteous deeds, our Lord and Savior Christ came and [?] in our minds.
He drove away from us the darkness of worshiping things made by human hands and led us to complete knowledge of the Holy Trinity: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
He also gave us the grace of the Spirit, through which we can bear and produce fruits of righteousness that please God the Creator.
But the pagans who worship the elements hold a great festival everywhere on this day, year after year,
because, that is, the sun has begun to prevail and its dominion to gain further degrees. They ought, however, to consider
that if the fact that the day now begins to gain on the night deserves any rejoicing and a great festival, then, in exactly the same way, the very same celebration is deserved
when, at another season, the night, the dominion of darkness, begins to gain on the day, the realm of the sun.
For just as human life would perish if the night, once it grew longer, did not turn and become shorter, so too, when the day begins to grow longer,
if it did not become shorter again, this world could not continue to exist. For without summer and winter, heat and cold, our way of life cannot be sustained in the life that [?].

For [?] to be completed [?]. These things are impossible without the sun’s ascent and descent and the lengthening and shortening of night and day. Therefore, the benefit we receive when the sun prevails
is precisely the same benefit we receive when it declines. The misguided pagans ought therefore either to hold a festival at both changes or at neither of them,
because the benefit from both is equal. And this comes from God, who arranged them in this way.
Chapter Eleven: An Exhortation concerning Good Conduct.
They, then, were holding a festival, as I said, for the sun, which at this season begins to overcome the dominion of darkness, but then declines again.
The holy Church, however, celebrates the birth of Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, who began to overcome error and Satan and never declined again.
Rather, his dominion has continued to gain ground, until all rational beings, visible and invisible, are brought into subjection
under his authority. For, it says, every knee shall bow to him, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those beneath the earth.
And just as our festivals are greater and more powerful than those of the pagans of every religion—for the truth of knowledge is found among us alone—so we ought
to have conduct grounded in the fear of God that is better and purer than that of the rest of humanity, taking equal care of both things:
the reading of the books and their interpretation, instruction concerning [?] and their occasions, and virtuous conduct that pleases Christ our Lord.
We should care for our companions and brothers more than for ourselves, if we truly are disciples of the apostles who emulated their Lord.
For all of them were concerned for our benefit, and they labored night and day,
in summer and winter, at sea and on land, by every means and in every way, so that all of us might be brought into the household of our Lord Christ
and obtain the good things prepared in heaven for those who believe rightly and conduct themselves properly. For they bravely faced every kind of suffering
and gave their lives over to death for our sake, because our life in Christ was more precious to them than their own life in this world. And what shall I say?
in this world. For one of them even chose to be excluded from the good things to come for the sake of all his brothers, so that they might share in the good things of Christ.
For he says, “I prayed that I myself might be accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers and my relatives according to the flesh, who are the children of Israel.”
If, then, blessed Paul prayed for harm to himself and almost for his own destruction for the sake of the common good,
how are we not disgraced and ashamed, and how do we not fall into great fear and trembling,
when we call ourselves their disciples but do not strive to match their conduct and their perfect intentions?
Instead, let us imitate the apostles, our teachers, in everything, as far as we can, so that we may share with them in the heavenly blessings.
For however much we study their teaching and profess their faith, if their conduct is not found in us, we do not reach the place to which they are going.
Instead, we become like blind people over whom the sun’s rays spread, but who do not enjoy their brightness because they have no organs capable of receiving their effects.
For in truth, good conduct is the demonstration of right faith and the confirmation of perfect teaching. Without [?], even our teaching is not believed by outsiders.
And we who are insiders, in turn, are not thought to learn it out of reverence for God. Instead, let us take care over our conduct and our love for one another.
Let us not become a cause of harm to ourselves and a stumbling block to everyone who sees us. Instead, let us prepare ourselves for good works,
so that we may be worthy of that declaration which says, “Come, you who are blessed by my Father, and inherit the kingdom that was prepared for you before the foundations of the world,”
together with all Christ’s righteous ones. To him be glory, and may his mercy be upon us forever. Amen.
Here ends the Explanation of the Nativity, composed by Mar
Thomas, the teacher of Edessa. May his prayer
be upon the sinner who wrote this. Amen.
